description: Hi! I'm Shiyin, a Year 3 Computing student at SMU (SCIS). We're building AURA: a health twin for astronauts on long missions. It learns each astronaut's own baseline, spots early compound risks (sleep, mood, radiation, heart rate), explains why, and guides self-care when Earth's 20+ min away. Looking for: React/Three.js (3D body), UI/UX design, someone with health/biology knowledge, and a storyteller for the pitch. Beginners welcome!
summary: AURA is an offline health twin for a simulated long-duration crew. When a message to Earth can take many minutes, the astronaut still needs a clear picture of how their own body is changing. AURA compares recent readings with that crew member's first two weeks, rather than with a population cutoff. Heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise, and radiation feed six body systems. Several mild drifts moving together can raise a system to amber or red even when no single number has crossed a personal limit. The screen explains the reason in plain language, offers self-care prompts while the link is delayed, and opens a flight-surgeon packet the crew can copy or save. A guided demo walks through a solar-particle event from a quiet day 60 to an amber day 64. Every number is simulated and labeled as an assumption. AURA is decision support for the story of the mission. It is not a medical device and it does not diagnose.
details:
Space Rockets built AURA, an offline health twin for a simulated long-duration crew. When a message to Earth can take many minutes, the astronaut still needs a clear picture of how their own body is changing.

AURA keeps a 180-day series for four fictional crew members. Each person has a personal baseline from days 1–14. Later readings are compared with that baseline, not with a population cutoff. Resting heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise, and radiation feed six body systems: heart, muscle and bone, brain, sleep, immune, and vision. One mild drift is scored lower than several drifts moving together. If that pattern holds for consecutive days, the system can show amber or red even when no single number has crossed a personal limit. Green, amber, and red are always paired with the words Quiet, Watch, or Review.

The screen names the reason in plain language. While the comm delay is on, or a system is amber or red, it shows self-care prompts. The crew can open a flight-surgeon packet, copy the text, or save a PDF. A guided walkthrough drives the real controls through a solar-particle story from a quiet day 60 to an amber day 64. A validation page compares the personal method with fixed bands on 200 simulated crews. Every numeric setting is stored as an assumption. Vision has no eye measurement, and muscle and bone has no scan. Those scores follow stand-in signals, and the panel says so.

The intended impact is a crew-facing decision aid for the story of a delayed mission, not a diagnosis and not a medical device. The team weighed communication delay, personal change versus population limits, colour that is never used alone, and an app that still runs with no network.

AURA is a React and TypeScript app built with Vite. The body is procedural Three.js geometry. State is stored with Zustand. Charts use Recharts. The packet PDF uses jsPDF. Tests run in Vitest. There is no backend and no downloaded 3D model.
